title: Sensors buried in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice catch neutrinos from deep space
body: On 6 October 2026 Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison won the Nobel Prize in Physics for IceCube, the South Pole observatory he first proposed in 1988. Neutrinos have no charge and almost no mass, so they pass through whole planets. Very rarely one hits an atomic nucleus in the ice and makes a charged particle that moves faster than light can in ice, about 76% of its speed in a vacuum, and like a boat outrunning its own waves it leaves a cone of blue Cherenkov light. **5,160 sensors** on 86 strings, between 1,450 and 2,450 metres deep, record when that light arrives, and the order of the hits gives the neutrino’s direction. Because neutrinos are not bent by magnetic fields or stopped by dust, they point back to the violent places that made them, as the [Nobel committee’s background](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/popular-physicsprize2026-1.pdf) explains.

slides.question: IceCube watches a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. How many light sensors hang in it?
slides.explanation: 5,160: 86 strings of 60 sensors each, lowered into holes melted with hot water, between 1,450 and 2,450 metres below the surface.

slides.alt: Animation in polar night. Under the South Pole snow, a cubic kilometre of ice fills with strings of light sensors. A neutrino comes up from below, hits a nucleus, and a muon streaks through with a blue cone of light; sensors light from red to purple. Then a sky map of the 2013, 2017 and 2023 finds.

slides.prompt: A neutrino’s muon has just crossed the ice. Turn your track until its timing matches the hits, and find its direction to within 3°.
slides.takeaway: Only one direction fits: the red sensors lit first, where the muon entered, the purple ones last. IceCube does this with all its sensors, to a fraction of a degree, and so traces the neutrino back across the sky.

slides.heading: From an idea to a new astronomy

events.text: A neutrino from a flaring blazar

slides.heading: Why the South Pole?
slides.text: Deep down the ice is dark, still and very clear: below 1,400 metres light can travel about 300 metres before it is absorbed. Unlike the sea, it has no glowing creatures, little radioactivity and no earthquakes, and a research station was already there. The catch: all drilling must be done in the short summer.

slides.question: Why do IceCube’s searches favour muon tracks that come up through the Earth?
options: The Earth blocks muons from the air
The ice is clearer at the bottom
slides.explanation: Cosmic rays hitting the air above make muons that reach the sensors, over a hundred million a day. The Earth stops them but not neutrinos, so a track from below almost surely began as a neutrino.
